content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a low-cost metric (proxy) that can be used to efficiently rank the architectures generated in the process of neural architecture search (NAS). It replaces the classifier part of each architecture with a transform layer and a frozen, untrained CONV layer, and trains this new architecture with a few iterations to match a synthesized 2D label. The training method has a few hyper-parameters, which can be searched for each downstream task to maximize the proxy's accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- This paper is well-motivated, and the introduction part is easy to read and understand.
- This paper is interesting and can be useful to the NAS community.
- The experiments are comprehensive. They cover different NAS benchmarks and different NAS algorithms. The proposed proxy consistently gives better results than chosen related works.

=============================================================================

Weakness:
- This paper needs to be revised. There are many essential details missing and mislabeled/unlabeled figures and tables.
  - Sec. 2.1 only mentions how to train an architecture with a few steps but doesn't tell how to use the results to rank architectures. If we evaluate the trained architectures on a given dataset and rank them, because Eproxy trains an architecture without its classifier (a typo in the paper: classfier), how do we get the classifier's weights, and what is the evaluation set? Missing this information makes this work unreproducible.
  - Fig. 2 is never referred to in the main text. After reading the figure and the caption, I still cannot get the point.
  - After reading the paper, it is unclear how to generate the label. The last sentence in Sec. 2.1 states the label is "the output of an untrained 6-layer FCN". What is the untrained 6-layer FCN? Any untrained 6-layer FCN? Does this FCN vary from evaluating one architecture to another? What is the impact of using different untrained FCNs?
  - The first sentence in Sec. 2.1 states "The Eproxy is designed for the architectures to learn the output of an untrained network on a set
of image-label pairs (See Fig. 4)." Is the label in the "image-label pairs" the same as "the output of an untrained network"? If not, how to use the label in Fig. 4?
  - Many ingredients in Fig. 4 are not explained. What are the switch-like things? What does the arrow with "evaluation hyperparameters" mean? How to do "feature combination" (Sec. 2.2-Item 2 only lists the choices of features, but doesn't mention how to "combine")?
  - The axes of Fig. 5 are not labeled nor explained. It is difficult to understand what this figure means.
  - Wrong figure reference in P.2 "Eproxy utilizes few-shot spatial-level regression on a set of image-label pairs (see Illustration in Fig. 3)."
  - What do the numbers in Table 1 mean? Are they MSEs as stated in the table or ranking correlations as mentioned in the caption?

- For the proposed Eproxy design:
  - Why can matching the architecture output to the output of an untrained 6-layer FCN serve as a good proxy metric? Any high-level explanation?
  - The explanation for why the proposed barrier layer works is that it makes the loss surface noisier, which is not necessarily translated to "better ranking". There are many other ways to serve the same purpose, such as data augmentation and weight noising, but (probably) not all of them can give a better ranking. Why can the barrier layer provide a better ranking? How does it compare with other methods, such as random data augmentation?
  - Is the barrier layer reinitialized per architecture? How does the random seed influence the performance of the barrier layer?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Reproducibility:
The paper needs to be revised to provide enough critical details. Currently, the reproducibility and clarity of the methodology are somewhat limited.

==================================================================

Novelty:
Marginally novel.

However, its writing and missing many important details make it difficult to reproduce and understand how/why the proposed method works.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents a novel design of a low-cost proxy for accuracy in neural architecture search by scoring architectures according to their performance on a carefully selected unsupervised task which requires only a couple of backward steps.
Specifically, randomly initialized networks are fed with inputs specific to a downstream task of interest - that is, the task on which we want to maximize performance of our network - and intermediate features are compared to various synthetic "taget" features, such as sine waves, samples from Rademacher distribution or features generated for the same input by a 6-layers-deep randomly initialized CNN network.
Each network that we want to score is trained to minimize MSE loss between its intermediate features and selected synthetic targets, in a few-shot manner (10 backward steps being a representative cost).
This proxy training is further regularized by incorporating a barrier layer, which is a randomly initialized convolutional layer used to transform any features that are subject to the MSE loss - unlike other parts, the barrier layer(s) is not subject to the proxy few-shot learning.
The method is called Efficient Proxy (Eproxy).
However, due to the relatively large number of hyperparameters in the proposed method (e.g., what synthetic features to use) the authors further propose to perform downstream-task-specific hyperparameter optimization (called DPS) to tune their Eproxy in an online manner - performing this HPO assumes access to a limited number of architectures fully trained on the downstream task, the results are denoted as Eproxy+DPS.
The method is evaluated on a number of NAS benchmarks, notably including recent benchmarks consisting of diverse downstream tasks, and on the DARTS CNN space (ImageNet).
The main benefit of the proposed method, as described in the paper, is its ability to work well on tasks not only limited to the typical ones (image classification being the most common example), and delivering strong performance in situations when existing zero-cost proxies fail.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strenghts:**

 - the method is interesting and, to the best of my knowledge, clearly novel
 - the paper tackles an important problem of robustifying low-cost NAS for tasks less common in NAS research but often important in real-world scenarios
 - the design of the method is sensible and simple
 - sufficiently good writing
 
**Weaknesses:**

 - (W1) Eproxy alone does not actually work that well, it is only Eproxy+DPS that delivers convincing results - however, the necessity of having extra trained architectures (even if only 20) puts this work in a significantly different complexity regime than most of the baselines to which the paper compares - in short, the choice of baselines seems inadequate to the cost of performing EProxy+DPS.
 - (W2) Related to the above, searching cost on ImageNet for Eproxy+DPS seems to ignore the necessity of training 20 architectures for DPS - including this cost would increase the searching time for Eproxy+DPS SIGNIFICANTLY, make it fall short to many of the baselines presented in Table 8 (e.g., TE-NAS, P-DARTS, likely SNAS and PC-DARTS).
 - (W3) Comparison to synflow and NASWOT in table 5 seems biased -- why only assume 0 queries for these method where both were originally proposed to be used with either random sampling or evolutionary search? Specifically, results reported for synflow in the original paper are between 51 and 34 queries to reach test accuracy of 94.22, which is significantly better than what is reported for Eproxy+DPS (150 queries). Also, it is unclear what the authors mean by "we utilize the Eproxy as the fitness function for Regularized Evolution" and then showing results for varying number of queries, especially 0 queries (this might be also related to the point below).
 - (W4) Showing that "Eproxy+DPS can find optimal global architectures within the RE search history" in Table 4 is incorrect in its context - it is possible that RE significantly helps Eproxy+DPS by prefiltering all architectures based on their accuracy (thus being very costly), showing results of Eproxy+DPS conditioned by running RE is not the same as showing results of just Eproxy+DPS (what the Table's caption suggests, by saying: "Eproxy+DPS uses substantially lower queries to find the global optimal architectures.")
 
**Minor shortcomings and suggestions:**

 - Figure 1 is not exactly informative as it does not convey any information about quality of each method
 - Figure 2 also does not seem to add much, I actually had pretty hard time understanding what it tries to say - what is "W" at x axis? why does "arch 1" finish earlier than "arch 2"? why do they follow the same curve? Just to be clear, I am quite sure I know what the authors tried to say here, the concept of cheap proxies for NAS is not hard to grasp, but the Figure in its current form is not helpful, in my opinion
 - while the choice of NAS benchmarks seems adequate to me, it would strengthen the paper if the authors could include experiments on some additional, large search spaces other than benchmarks/DARTS, for example a MobileNet-like search space
 - zero-cost proxies considered in the paper are not very new, some of the more recent ones that the authors could include to make comparison more convincing are: ZenNAS, KNAS
 - I would suggest changing the title - in its current form it is unclear really what the authors tried to say, some reasoning: 1) it is unclear if the authors mean a particular efficient proxy or efficient proxies in general, "is" suggests that it is a particular proxy, but then there is not proxy called "Efficient Proxy", which suggests that it is rather referring to a family of efficient proxies; 2) however, saying that a generic class of efficient proxies is now extensible suggests that the authors propose a generic method to make any efficient proxy extensible, which is not the case. I would recommend changing the title to something like "Extensible and Efficient Proxy for NAS", or something similar, it would make it much clear that the authors propose a new proxy that is supposed to be both efficient and extensible.
 - Actually, another minor comment is that I am not sure if "extensible" is the best term here -- in my opinion a better term would be: "generalizable", "transferable" or "adaptive", all of them suggest to me some kind of changes in the training data (i.e., downstream task), which seems to be the main point of Eproxy. At the same time, "extensible" suggests more that something new could be easily added to the proposed method in order to make it better.
 

 
**Details:**

_W1:_ Specifically, on NDS Eproxy is only comparable to NASWOT, despite performing few-shot training of architectures (i.e., even if the absolute cost is not very high, it's still 10x more costly than NASWOT, without any obvious benefits), furthermore on TransNAS-Bench-Micro Eproxy fails quite significantly on 6 out of 7 tasks.
On NAS-Bench-MR Eproxy achieves convincing improvement (i.e., better in at least one metric - spearman-r or top% models - while not compromising another) over the selected baselines in only 2 out of 9 cases, consequently it falls short to synflow on average.
On the other hand, as mentioned above, Eproxy+DPS does improve upon both synflow and naswot, most of the time, but it also requires training a number of architecture, which makes it no longer low-cost method - at best, it should be treated as efficient, predictor-based approach.
However, the comparison is done almost exclusively with methods that do not assume any training (the only notable exceptions are Table 6, 7, and 8, but they have their own problems, as mentioned in other parts of the review, and the choice of baselines in Table 6 and 7 is not also not _very_ convincing).

_W2:_ reported searching cost is approximately 1.5 GPU hours (0.06 GPU days) but training a single model from the DARTS CNN space on CIFAR-10, using the official code, takes roughly a day on a V100. Even though the authors use models from a different search space (NDS-DARTS benchmark), that in practice come for free, and might also be cheaper to train than standard DARTS, I am not convinced that the presented results are fair in comparing the proposed methods vs. baselines. Specifically, considering that the main focus of the submitted work is to enable low-cost NAS for diverse tasks, it is not unreasonable in my opinion to expect the proposed method to work well in situations when we do not have a priori knowledge of performance of certain architectures, or even if there exists a highly-correlated proxy task/search space (like DARTS vs. NDS-DARTS). Therefore not including the cost of obtaining accuracy for the 20 architectures needed to conduct DPS is likely to be misleading, were the method to be applied in real-world situations, which it tries to address.

_W4:_ to be clear, I am inclined to believe that Eproxy+DPS is likely to produce better results than just using RE, especially if the authors used it to augment RE, like, e.g., Abdelfattah et al. However, formally speaking, this has not been shown in the current paper. Specifically, if we know that RE finds optimal architecture in N steps, then "finding optimal architecture within RE history" is actually a problem of finding the correct model within the N models, rathar than within the whole search space -- the a priori knowledge that the optimal models exists in a relatively small subset of the search space provides a very strong prior which can naturally boost a method's performance. In the context of Table 7, RE is shown to find the optimal architecture in ~560 queries, so Eproxy+DPS needing 58 actually explores 10% of all models - if we were to apply the same level of performance to the entire search space (15k models) then it would be 1500 queries. While I would not claim that this is the expected number for Eproxy+DPS, I hope that this clearly shows why the current results are misleading. Even a random search would do significantly better in this setting.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clearly written and novel, but quality of the evaluation leaves a lot of doubts. See strengths and weaknesses for more details.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In general, I like the direction this paper takes and that it tries to address a relevant problem for zero/low-cost NAS.
At the same time, the design of the method makes a lot of sense to me (intuitively) and represents an interesting direction for potential future research.
However, when it comes to the evaluation of the proposed method I have a lot of doubts whether it really adequately characterizes performance of the proposed method.
In short, I have reservations about pretty much every single reported result (details can be found in the main review), therefore it is impossible for me to confidently say what performance would be expected from the proposed method and how it compares to the _relevant_ state-of-the-art methods.
Considering that, I am afraid I have no other choice than to reject the paper in its current form.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an efficient proxy for NAS based on two things: (1) a barrier layer that contributes to making the proxy task more difficult (thereby allowing better distinction among various architectures), and (2) a proxy task that exploits evolutionary algorithms to refine the search. Experiments are conducted on many NAS-Bench tasks, search spaces, and datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper has following strengths:

1. The idea of using a simple barrier layer to distinguish the architectures is useful and interesting.

2. Experiments are truly comprehensive across many tasks and NAS-Benches.

3. Compared to predictor-based NAS, the accuracy of the proposed methods is good (and saves compute time)


The paper has following weaknesses:

1. The technique is not truly zero-shot, yet most of the comparisons have been made against zero-shot proxies or older NAS methods. Given that the authors do train on some proxy tasks, I would expect them to compare against better NAS methods (and not the methods that other existing truly-zero-shot NAS methods compare to). Also, one of the main problems with zero-shot NAS and other related techniques (that aim to do NAS in a very short time) is scalability. For instance, in 0.5-1 GPU hour, Eproxy (with DPS, etc.) is able to achieve competitive accuracies as PC-DARTS, etc. If we were to allow a constraint of, say, 24-30 GPU hours, would we be able to obtain accuracies close to those of methods like DONNA (https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.08859), alpha-divergence-based NAS (https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07954), etc.? Specifically, my question is to explore scalability of the proposed method (and that of other zero-shot proxies). Given more time, would we be able to improve the solution to match more expensive techniques? Or is the best we can get with efficient methods is whatever we get within the first GPU hour (and cannot be improved further)? 

2. Appendix A7: Loss difference between best and worst network on NAS-Bench-101 (due to the use of barrier layer) is 0.01 (see Fig. 7); thus, for any network that performs somewhere in the middle of best and worst, the loss difference would be even lower. I am not convinced that this is sufficient to differentiate among architectures’ performance. But obviously, the barrier layer helps with the correlations, etc. Can the authors investigate why the barrier layer really helps? Authors have provided very little intuition behind the barrier layer which is the main contribution of this paper. It may have something to do with changing shapes of optimization landscape as the authors allude to (not sure how to systematically study it, some thoughts are given in point 4 below, if applicable). A better understanding of this phenomenon would make this paper very strong.

3. It was also recently pointed out that for most NAS-Benches, number of parameters and number of FLOPS alone achieve significantly better correlation than most of the zero-cost proxies (https://iclr-blog-track.github.io/2022/03/25/zero-cost-proxies/). I would like the authors to compare against these naïve baselines to make sure that we are not seeing spurious correlations.

4. A few important papers are missing from discussion: ZenNAS (https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01063, ICCV 2021) and NN-Mass (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00780, CVPR 2021). Authors must cite both papers and discuss in detail. ZenNAS is another zero-shot proxy that must be compared against. NN-Mass is a more theoretical work but was one of the pioneering works on zero-shot proxies (authors can try to use some of the concepts used by NN-Mass to better understand the gradient flow properties to analyze the role of the barrier layer, if applicable).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Paper is very interesting, high quality in terms of number of experiments (although a few important ones are missing), and original.
content.summary_of_the_review: Some important comparisons are missing. If the authors can better understand the role of barrier layer, that would make this paper very strong. Currently, the scalability experiment (i.e., comparison to methods like DONNA), comparison to ZenNAS, and better understanding of barrier layer are most critical. If they are sufficiently addressed, I will raise my score.
